Neonates of the Patagonian chinchilla mouse emerge at a remarkably small wet weight of approximately 2 grams [Wwb = approximately 2 grams], a value that underscores the altricial nature of this sigmodontine rodent. This modest mass at birth stands in contrast to the considerably larger ultimate adult wet weight attained by males, which has been documented at up to 65 grams [Wwi = up to 65 grams] in field-captured specimens from the southern Andean steppe. Males thus undergo a roughly thirtyfold increase in body mass from birth to adulthood, reflecting a growth trajectory that must accommodate the energetic demands of a cold, resource-poor environment. The neonatal mass of 2 grams [Wwb = 2 grams] is notably low relative to other members of the subfamily Sigmodontinae of similar adult size, suggesting that the species invests minimally in individual offspring at parturition, likely offsetting this with a relatively rapid postnatal growth phase. Field records also indicate that some adult males may plateau at around 50 grams under less favorable conditions, though the upper extreme of 65 grams [Wwi = 65 grams] is consistently recovered from high-quality habitats of the Patagonian interior. This pronounced variation in ultimate body mass likely reflects differences in local primary productivity and the duration of the active foraging season across the species' fragmented range.

When expressed relative to the species' average adult mass, this metabolic rate supports the view that small, cold-adapted mammals must sustain heightened oxidative capacities to maintain endothermy. Maximum longevity records for the Patagonian chinchilla mouse indicate a lifespan of approximately 5.5 years [am = approximately 5.5 years] under optimal captive conditions at a stable core temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This lifespan is notably extended for a small-bodied sigmodontine rodent, many of which rarely exceed two to three years in the wild or captivity. This extended potential lifespan, combined with early maturation and prolific reproduction, positions the species as an intermediate on the slow-fast continuum of mammalian life-history strategies.
